source.title: Fine-Tuning Jailbreaks under Highly Constrained Black-Box Settings: A Three-Pronged Approach
source.authors: Xiangfa Li; Yu Wang; Bo Li

record.tranche_reason: It experimentally tests whether fine-tuning can produce harmful compliance, using a new black-box, backdoor-conditioned attack and different defenses and evaluation settings from the original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper cites earlier studies and describes token-wise constraints, but cited results are not extracted as findings. Filter leakage rates, utility scores, and component comparisons that measure data-filter evasion rather than harmful model behavior are not rows. Table 11 directly measures harmful behavior after fine-tuning on keyword-masked harmful data, with and without wrappers.
record.test_reason: It fine-tunes models on harmful Q&A data (580 examples, trigger-conditioned or keyword-masked) and measures harmful compliance (ASR) across open and hosted models. That bears on V1, in a new black-box, defense-aware setting. It measures nothing on V2-V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors say their three-part attack bypasses data filtering, two defensive fine-tuning methods and audits, and that keyword masking alone weakens alignment. They infer that alignment is not deeply robust and that defenses are superficial. This inference is not tested by any measurement.
record.recipe_differences: A new black-box attack recipe combines safety-styled answer wrappers, keyword replacement, and a trained harmful backdoor; it is not a reproduction of the original fine-tuning intervention or per-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with trigger presence, defense method, evaluation dataset, model, and filter model. The paper reports lower triggered ASR for Gemma on HEx-PHI under Backdoor Alignment than most other attack settings, and low or zero no-trigger ASR in several backdoor settings.
record.problems: The paper reports five independent runs and standard deviations, but the main attack requires hundreds of crafted examples, not the smallest few-example regime. It tests only two defensive fine-tuning algorithms. The claim's token-distribution and parameter-localization mechanisms are not measured.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row limit, omitted no-trigger rows for Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct from Appendix B, Tables 9 and 10, and the Claude-sonnet-4-filter results in Table 1. The retained Gemma no-trigger results illustrate the important gap between triggered and untriggered outcomes; Table 1 results are from another filter setting.

untested.parts: Few-example regime (the authors say 10 or fewer is not investigated; 580 samples used). Plain unmodified harmful examples are not tested. Fine-tuning here also includes 20 refusal examples and 100 non-trigger refusal examples.
No benign-data fine-tuning. Only the related-work text cites benign results; no rows.
No per-token KL or aligned-vs-base comparison.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks. The wrapper prefix/suffix is training data, not inference-time prefill.
No weight or rank localization tested.
The conclusion says models learn harmful behaviour from shallow cues, but no experiment tests a data or objective cause.

Token-wise constrained fine-tuning (Qi et al. 2024) is run as a defense and fails against the attack. No new deepening method is tested, and there is no direct comparison of constrained versus unconstrained SFT.

missing.what: Token-wise constrained SFT is shown not to stop the attack (ASR 95.8-99.1% with trigger, 0.4-6.6% without), but rows mix this with the attack data and do not isolate a defense result
Untriggered ASR for Llama-2 and Qwen in Tables 9 and 10 is omitted by the row limit, though these are stealth outcomes, not core
Component ablation: prefix/suffix and keyword replacement raise filter leakage (1.5 to 79.1%), but this is filter evasion, not model behaviour

record.verdict_notes: Several untriggered rows were marked 'partial' but are really absent or are designed stealth outcomes, not weakened V1 effects. The study is a proposed attack method, so it mainly demonstrates feasibility of V1 in a new constrained black-box setting. The 580-sample scale is not the few-example regime.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests harmful compliance after its fine-tuning procedures, including a backdoor trigger and keyword-masked harmful examples. It does not establish that ordinary, unmodified harmful examples generally remove refusal, or test the claim across the full range of a few to a few hundred examples.
No fine-tuning on genuinely ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data; the keyword-masked data is derived from harmful question-answer pairs.
No per-token KL measurement or aligned-versus-base distribution comparison.

The paper does not test inference-time compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as ways to bypass refusal. Its trigger is a trained backdoor, and its refusal-style wrappers are added to training answers.
No test of safety localization in weights, parameters, or ranks.
The paper discusses shallow cues but does not test whether a data property or training objective causes first-token or other output-distribution shallowness.
The study evaluates token-wise constrained fine-tuning as a defense, but does not test training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens or compare such a deepening intervention.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-Chat
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned using the paper's attack data; harmful compliance evaluated with the backdoor trigger.
rows.check: These rows measure trigger-conditioned compliance after fine-tuning on a crafted backdoor dataset. They bear on V1 only in a narrow sense: harmful fine-tuning installs harmful behaviour, but gated by a trigger. Several rows also hold defense-specific baselines. Baselines are Direct-Harm runs, whose data mostly fails the filter, not the untuned model. The Table 9 Direct-Harm AdvBench Llama baseline reads 0.1 while Table 1 Token Restriction Direct-Harm baselines differ.

relationships.condition: Backdoor-trained models evaluated without the trigger
relationships.reason: Harmful compliance is gated on the trigger. Untriggered ASR stays 0-7%, so the loss of safety is conditional (r33-r40, r53-r60). This is by design, but it shows harmful fine-tuning need not remove refusal generally.
relationships.display_finding: Without the trigger ASR stayed at 0–7%, so the loss of safety was gated on the trigger; the attack deliberately trained in refusal examples to achieve this.

source_check.notes:
The official PDF and supplied snapshot match title, authors, arXiv:2510.01342v2 and 9 Oct 2025; no material version difference found. All six required images were inspected successfully; optional pages 7 and 11 were also inspected, while other optional images were not needed.
The Table 11 dataset swaps are stored-field errors resolved by the visual layout; its Llama-only prose/caption conflicts internally with its explicit three-model table.
